Who Should Design the Summer Project?

Every June, my cousin used to come home with the same packet: forty pages of reading passages and math review, stapled at the corner, due the first day of school. Every August, usually in the last four days before the deadline, he filled it out at the kitchen table while complaining loudly. He finished it each year, and I doubt he could have told you a single thing that was in it by October. That packet is the main reason I believe summer projects should be designed by students, with teachers setting the boundaries instead of the content.

The strongest argument for student design is simple. Summer work only happens if the student decides to do it. During the school year a teacher can check in daily, answer questions, and notice when someone is falling behind. In July nobody is watching. A project a student picked has a much better chance of surviving ten weeks without supervision than one handed down from above. A girl who loves cooking might spend the summer testing how changing the amount of baking soda affects a batch of cookies, recording the results, and writing up what she found. She would be practicing measurement, ratios, and the scientific method, and she would be doing it because she wanted to know the answer. The same girl given a worksheet on ratios would do it the night before it was due.

Student design also teaches something that teacher-designed work cannot, which is how to plan. Choosing a topic, deciding what the finished product should look like, and breaking the work into pieces are skills that students are rarely asked to use, because the assignment sheet normally does all of that for them. Colleges and employers expect people to manage open-ended tasks. A summer project is a low-risk place to try it. If a student picks a topic that turns out to be too big, such as building a working app with no coding experience, and has to scale it back to a simple quiz game, that is a real lesson about scope, and one that costs nothing more than a few frustrating weeks.

There is also a fairness issue that people overlook. Students spend their summers very differently. Some travel, some work thirty hours a week, some watch younger siblings all day, and some have no reliable internet. A single teacher-designed project assumes a single kind of summer. A student who works at a family restaurant could design a project around tracking the restaurant's busiest hours and proposing a better staffing schedule. That project fits into the life the student already has, where a required museum visit or online research assignment might not.

The usual objection is that students will choose something easy or will not cover what the school needs them to learn. This is a fair worry, and it is why teachers should not disappear from the process. A teacher can require a written proposal in May, list the skills the project has to show, such as research from at least three sources or a certain amount of writing, and hand out a rubric in advance. A proposal to "watch movies all summer" gets sent back; a proposal to compare three film adaptations to the novels they came from gets approved. The teacher guards the standards while the student supplies the idea.

Teachers know what students need to learn, but students know what they will actually do in the middle of July. A summer project only works when both are true at once, and letting students design the project inside a teacher's framework is the most reliable way to get there.
